ety.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian اَخْتَر (axtar), from Middle Persian 𐭠𐭧𐭲𐭫 (ʾhtl /⁠axtar⁠/), an ancient backformation from 𐭠𐭯𐭠𐭧𐭲𐭫 (ʾpʾhtl /⁠abāxtar⁠/, “planet”), due to a mistaken folk etymology that the first element ab- was a negative suffix, since Zoroastrianism considers the planets to be nefarious "un-stars" due to their astronomically odd behavior.

s.g: a unisex given name, Akhtar, from Persian

ety.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian اَخْتَر (axtar), from Middle Persian 𐭠𐭧𐭲𐭫 (ʾhtl /⁠axtar⁠/), an ancient backformation from 𐭠𐭯𐭠𐭧𐭲𐭫 (ʾpʾhtl /⁠abāxtar⁠/, “planet”), due to a mistaken folk etymology that the first element ab- was a negative suffix, since Zoroastrianism considers the planets to be nefarious "un-stars" due to their astronomically odd behavior.

Semi-learned borrowing from Sanskrit आर्द्रक (ārdraka, “ginger”) through Prakrit *𑀆𑀤𑁆𑀤𑀅 (*āddaa), from आर्द्र (ārdra, “wet”), as fresh ginger is wet. Doublet of आदा (ādā). Tom Hoogervorst instead proposes it and other Indic terms are from Proto-Malayic *halia.
Learned borrowing from Sanskrit अभिनन्दन (abhinandana); equivalent to अभि- (abhi-) + नंदन (nandan).

s.g: Imphal (a city, the state capital of Manipur, India)
Cape Verde (an archipelago and country in West Africa)

ety.text: Inherited from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *खद्ध (khaddha, “pit, ditch, manure pit”), an alternative form of खाअ (khāa, “dug up, pit, ditch”), from Sanskrit खात (khāta, “excavated”). The -द्धा (-ddhā) suffix is by analogy to other past participles like णद्ध (ṇaddha, “tied”) and बद्ध (baddha, “bound”). Doublet of खात (khāt).

x: और तब उन्होंने बताया कि खाना […] भसका जाता है बहुत तेज़ी से हाथ चलाकर, चारों ओर खिंडाते हुए और हाथ-मुँह को सानते हुए।

ety.text: Hindi verb set खिंडना (khiṇḍnā) खिंडाना (khiṇḍānā) खिंडवाना (khiṇḍvānā) Transitive form of खिंडना (khiṇḍnā) with the suffix -आना (-ānā).

s.g: gulal, abir, a coloured powder especially used during the Holi festival
a type of cannon carried on the back of a horse
to cause one to climb, ascend

ety.text: Inherited from Prakrit चित्त (citta, “mind”), from Sanskrit चित्त (citta, “heart, mind < longing < noticed”), from the root चित् (cit, “to notice”). Doublet of चित्त (citt). Related to चीतना (cītnā, “to think”), चेतना (cetnā, “consciousness”), and the latter part of बातचीत (bātcīt).
From छोड़ना (choṛnā, “to leave”) or छोरना (chornā, “to free”).

From Bengali টিকা (ṭika), from Sanskrit तिलक (tilaka, “tilak”). In medieval Bengal, among many techniques, variolaters would make an incision upon the forehead, in which smallpox powder was rubbed. Such marks were known as টিকা (ṭika) on account of the resemblance to a tilak. Compare also the borrowed टीकादार (ṭīkādār).
Borrowed from Sanskrit त्रिज्या (trijyā). By surface analysis, त्रि- (tri-) + ज्या (jyā). Cognate with Marathi त्रिज्या (trijyā).
Borrowed from Classical Persian دَرْیَائِی (daryā'ī), from دَرْیَا (daryā) + ـِی (-ī). By surface analysis, दर्या (daryā) + -ई (-ī).

x: उसके दौरे से ठीक पहले उसकी गिरफ़्तारी हो गई।

ety.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian دوره (dawra), from Arabic دَوْرَة (dawra).
Learned borrowing from New Sanskrit नगण्य (nagaṇya). By surface analysis, न- (na-) + गण्य (gaṇya).

s.g: after you (a gesture, usually polite, urging another person to take a turn at something ahead of the speaker)
Parvati, the goddess of fertility, love and devotion also the wife of Lord Shiva
x: देवी पार्वती को शक्ति का अवतार माना जाता है।

s.g: a female given name, Parvati, from Sanskrit

ety.text: Borrowed from Portuguese pera (“pear”). Cognate with Bengali পেয়ারা (peẏara), Malayalam പേര (pēra), Gujarati પેરુ (peru), Marathi पेरू (perū), Swahili pera.
Inherited from Apabhramsa 𑀧𑀺𑀬𑀸𑀭𑀬 (piyāraya-, “dear”), Sanskrit प्रियकारा (priyakārā, “agreeable”), from प्रिय (priya) + कार (kāra). By surface analysis, पियार (piyār) + -आ (-ā).

s.g: the act of perception, being visible
alternative spelling of प्रारंभ करना (prārambh karnā)

ety.text: Perhaps from बनिया (baniyā, “merchant”), characterizing their usual clothing.
Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀪𑀢𑁆𑀢 (bhatta), from Sanskrit *भार्त (*bhārta), vriddhi of भृत (bhṛta, “servant”). See भाड़ा (bhāṛā) for more. Cognate with Marathi भत्ता (bhattā).
Hindi verb set मरना (marnā) मारना (mārnā) मराना (marānā) मरवाना (marvānā) Causative form of मरना (marnā) with the suffix -आना (-ānā).

x: गुंडे ने मुझे पीठ पर बहुत ज़ोर से मारा।

ety.text: Hindi verb set मरना (marnā) मारना (mārnā) मराना (marānā) मरवाना (marvānā) Inherited from Sanskrit मारयति (mārayati), from the root मृ (mṛ). Cognate with Nepali मार्नु (mārnu), Assamese মাৰা (mara).
Borrowed from Classical Persian مُنَقّیٰ (munaqqā), from Arabic مُنَقَّى (munaqqā). Compare Marathi मनुका (manukā).
Hindi verb set मूतना (mūtnā) मुताना (mutānā) Inherited from Sanskrit मूत्रयति (mūtrayati). Cognate with Gujarati મૂતરવું (mūtarvũ), Marathi मुतणे (mutṇe), Assamese মূতা (muta), Sylheti ꠝꠥꠔꠣ (muta).
Sanskritic formation from मूल्य (mūlya, “value”) + मीमांसा (mīmānsā, “reflection, examination, profound thought”).

s.g: a burring guttural sound, the letter ra (as so pronounced)

x: पदोन्नति का निर्णय वरिष्ठता के आधार पर लिया गया।
अपनी वरिष्ठता का अनुभव करने के लिए उसे किसी प्रमाण की आवश्यकता न थी।

s.g: Ecclesiastes (a book in the Old Testament of the Bible)
washing of an elephant; (figuratively) used to indicate a useless or unproductive work

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit हस्तिस्नान (hastisnāna). By surface analysis, हस्तिन् (hastin, “elephant”) + स्नान (snāna, “bathing, washing”).
